title: The ads go dark
takeaway: Before changing your move, ask what others can still do.

start.title: Who gains when the ads disappear?
start.line: Cigarette ads were banned from TV and radio. Would you expect established companies to lose—or benefit?
dialogue: Cigarette ads were banned from TV and radio.
Would you expect established cigarette companies to lose money—or benefit?

experiment.title: The ban has not happened yet. What will you do?
experiment.line: Your rival will keep advertising. You can keep your ads or stop paying for them. In this example, customers spend the same total; ads change which company gets their money.
dialogue: Your rival will keep advertising.
In this example, customers spend the same total. Ads change which company gets their money.
Will you keep your ads—or stop paying for them?

keep.title: You keep your sales—and your bill.
keep.line: You both still pay for advertising. Your money stays at 60.
dialogue: You kept your sales—and your ad bill. You still have 60 left.
Would you like to compare stopping, or see what the ban changes?

stop.title: The bill vanished. So did some sales.
stop.line: You saved 40 on ads, but lost 60 in sales. Your rival still reaches customers.
dialogue: Your ad bill disappeared. But customers moved to your rival.
You saved 40 on ads, but lost 60 in sales. You kept 40.

ban.title: Now neither company can advertise.
ban.line: Neither has the advantage of advertising alone. Each keeps 100 in this made-up example.

visual.phase: Now the ban applies to both companies

dialogue: Now the ban stops both companies’ ads.
Your rival no longer has the advantage of advertising alone. You each keep 100.

compare.title: Same move. Different result.
compare.line: Your ads are off in both pictures. What changes your result?
dialogue: Your ads are off in both pictures.
What changed your result from 40 to 100?

bill.title: Your bill was zero both times.
bill.line: Look at the rival’s TV. That is what changed.

cause.title: Strategic interdependence
cause.line: Your result depends on your choices AND other people’s choices. Your move alone cannot explain what you get.
dialogue: Your result depends on your choices AND other people’s choices.
That’s strategic interdependence. Your choice alone doesn’t explain what you get.

history.title: Who already has recognition?
history.line: A familiar brand and a newcomer both lose TV ads. Which already has customers who recognise its name?
dialogue: Back to the real ban. Here’s another way established companies could benefit.
Which brand already has customers who recognise its name?

historyyes.title: A different way the restriction could help.
historyyes.line: Yes. Familiar brands already had recognition. Losing an advertising channel could make entry harder. Other advertising channels remained.

historyno.title: A different way the restriction could help.
historyno.line: The established brand already had recognition. The newcomer still had to build it. Losing an advertising channel could make entry harder. Other advertising channels remained.

evidence.title: Investors expected benefits.
evidence.line: Stock-market evidence suggested established firms could benefit. Our coins illustrate a possibility; they are not historical results.

limit.title: What if customers buy much less?
limit.line: We kept spending fixed. Would the saved advertising bill still guarantee a gain?
dialogue: Our experiment kept total customer spending fixed.
If customers bought much less, would the saved ad bill still guarantee a gain?

limitno.title: The assumption matters.
limitno.line: A lower bill is not enough if income falls by more.

limityes.title: The assumption matters.
limityes.line: Exactly. Compare lost income with the saved advertising cost.

end.title: Strategic interdependence
end.line: Before changing your move, ask what others can still do.

predict_loss.title: You expect them to lose business.
predict_loss.line: That makes sense: without TV ads, they lose a way to reach customers. But their competitors lose that way too. Let’s test how those two changes interact.

choices.label: Go back to before the ban

dialogue: You expect them to lose business. Without ads, they lose a way to reach customers.
But their rivals lose that way too. Let’s see why that matters.

predict_benefit.title: You think the ban could help.
predict_benefit.line: There could be a benefit when competitors lose the same option. Let’s test one way that might happen, rather than assume it must.

choices.label: Go back to before the ban

dialogue: You think the ban could help them.
Let’s test one way that could happen. We won’t assume it must.

predict_unsure.title: It could pull in two directions.
predict_unsure.line: Ads bring in business, but they also cost money. And the ban affects competitors too. Let’s separate those effects.

choices.label: Go back to before the ban

dialogue: Ads bring in business, but they also cost money.
The ban changes both companies’ options. Let’s investigate.

before_ban.title: Before the ban, both companies can advertise.
before_ban.line: We’re switching to a made-up example. You run the company on the left. First, see what you keep while both companies advertise.

visual.receipt: 100 from customers − 40 spent on ads = 60 left

choices.label: Try a decision before the ban

dialogue: Let’s go back to before the ban. Both companies can still advertise.
This is a made-up example. You run the company on the left.
You receive 100 coins from customers and spend 40 on ads. That leaves 60.
